subject: Physiology
subtopic: ABO and Rh blood group physiology and transfusion compatibility
concept: Blood groups are inherited antigenic systems expressed on red blood cells and other blood components. The ABO and Rh systems are especially important because antibodies against incompatible antigens can cause clinically significant transfusion reactions.

content.definition: The ABO blood group system classifies individuals according to A and B carbohydrate antigens on the red-cell surface and corresponding naturally occurring antibodies in plasma. The Rh system includes several protein antigens, with D being the principal antigen used to classify a person as Rh-positive or Rh-negative.
content.explanation: In the ABO system, group A red cells express A antigen and plasma normally contains anti-B; group B expresses B antigen and has anti-A; group AB expresses both A and B antigens and normally lacks anti-A and anti-B; group O lacks A and B antigens and normally has both anti-A and anti-B. ABO antibodies are predominantly IgM with some IgG components and can activate complement. RhD is different: anti-D is generally an immune antibody produced after exposure rather than a naturally occurring antibody, and is predominantly IgG. Rh antibodies can cross the placenta and can cause hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
content.mechanism: ABO compatibility depends on preventing recipient antibodies from binding donor red-cell antigens. An ABO-incompatible red-cell transfusion can produce antibody-mediated agglutination and complement-associated intravascular hemolysis. Blood typing commonly uses forward typing to identify A and B antigens on patient RBCs and reverse typing to detect expected anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma. RhD typing identifies whether D antigen is present. Antibody screening and crossmatching provide additional compatibility assessment before transfusion.
content.structure: ABO antigens are carbohydrate structures carried on glycoproteins and glycolipids of the RBC membrane. The ABO locus has major A, B and O allelic forms; A and B encode functional glycosyltransferases, whereas common O alleles produce little or no functional A/B transferase. Rh antigens are membrane proteins; the clinically most important Rh antigen is D.
content.function: Blood group antigens are inherited cell-surface markers with important immunohematologic significance. Their normal physiological functions are not fully established for ABO antigens, while Rh proteins may contribute to RBC membrane biology and transport functions.
content.clinical_relevance: ABO and Rh compatibility are essential in transfusion medicine. ABO-incompatible RBC transfusion can cause an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. RhD alloimmunization is important in transfusion and pregnancy because maternal anti-D IgG can cross the placenta and destroy RhD-positive fetal RBCs in subsequent or sensitized pregnancies.
content.diagnosis: Blood grouping uses serologic ABO and RhD typing. ABO forward typing detects RBC antigens and reverse typing detects expected plasma antibodies. Pretransfusion testing also includes an antibody screen and, when indicated, a serologic crossmatch.
content.treatment: Management of an incompatible or hemolytic transfusion reaction requires immediate recognition, stopping the transfusion and urgent clinical and transfusion-service evaluation. Prevention relies on correct patient identification, blood typing, antibody screening, compatibility testing and selection of appropriate blood components. RhD alloimmunization in pregnancy can be prevented in appropriate RhD-negative pregnant patients with anti-D immunoprophylaxis according to clinical guidelines.
high_yield: ABO groups are A, B, AB and O.
Group A: A antigen on RBCs, anti-B in plasma.
Group B: B antigen on RBCs, anti-A in plasma.
Group AB: A and B antigens, no expected anti-A or anti-B.
Group O: no A or B antigens, both anti-A and anti-B.
ABO antibodies can cause severe acute hemolytic transfusion reactions when incompatible RBCs are transfused.
Rh-positive means D antigen is present; Rh-negative means D antigen is absent.
Anti-D is generally an immune IgG antibody produced after exposure and can cause hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
Forward typing tests RBC antigens; reverse typing tests expected ABO antibodies in plasma.
Crossmatching is performed to further assess donor-recipient compatibility before transfusion.

terminology.etymology: Rh system designation; D is the major clinically important antigen.
